evidence.title: Guiding Clostridioides difficile Infection Prevention Efforts in a Hospital Setting With AI
evidence.outcome: Adherence to bundle components by workflow fit
evidence.effect: Components integrated into existing pharmacist workflows were used and reduced antimicrobial use; multistage new-behavior hand hygiene component had low adherence and failed.
evidence.quote: In contrast, our efforts had the greatest association with antimicrobial stewardship, likely because the AI guidance was integrated into current workflows of pharmacists.

evidence.title: Integrating AI into Clinical Workflows: A Simulation Study on Implementing AI-aided Same-day Diagnostic Testing Following an Abnormal Screening Mammogram
evidence.venue: AMIA ... Annual Symposium proceedings. AMIA Symposium
evidence.effect: Minimal disruption: 4% reduction in daily patient volume or 2% increase in operating time under specified conditions.
evidence.quote: Using discrete simulation, we found minimal disruption to the workflow (a 4% reduction in daily patient volume or a 2% increase in operating time) under specific conditions: operation from 9 am to 12 pm with all radiologists managing all patient types (screenings, diagnostics, and biopsies).

evidence.title: Direct deep learning analysis of three-dimensional automated breast ultrasound videos with reading mode optimization for breast cancer diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Reading time by AI reading mode
evidence.effect: Concurrent reading reduced mean time by 13.5 seconds vs independent and 33.6 seconds vs second-reading; both P<0.001.
evidence.quote: Compared with both independent-reading and second-reading, concurrent-reading resulted in significantly shorter reading times for all radiologists, with mean differences of 13.5 seconds (95% confidence interval [CI], 12.7 to 14.2; P<0.001) and 33.6 seconds (95% CI, 32.5 to 34.6; P<0.001), respectively ( Table 3 ).
evidence.sample_unit: patients (test set; 547 total, read by 6 radiologists)

evidence.title: Randomized trial of electronic health record implemented AI risk prediction in kidney transplant care
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported tool utilization and workflow barriers
evidence.effect: Utilization averaged 29%, SD 37%; one physician reported 100%, remaining physicians 0–30%. Reported barriers included time constraints, a separate EHR tab, absent high-risk alerts, and no perceived clinical consequence.
evidence.quote: The reported utilization differed highly between physicians (one physician reported 100% utilization, while all remaining physicians reported 0–30%; mean 29%, SD 37%), precluding meaningful stratified analysis by clinician-level uptake.

evidence.title: Identifying risk factors for drug use recurrence with ecological momentary assessment, wearable technologies, and machine learning: a feasibility trial of peer recovery support specialist intervention
evidence.outcome: Data-collection compliance and participant and staff workflow burden
evidence.effect: Across 229 participants, compliance declined from ∼41 days during Baseline to ∼30 days during Phase 1 to ∼21 days during Phase 2; daily entries and alert-response calls were burdensome.
evidence.quote: Important aspects related to feasibility included difficulties with learning how to use the RNI Health app, the high burden of daily entries with the RNI Health app, limited battery life of the wearable devices, loss of wearable devices, and the high burden of responding by phone to numerous alerts generated by the algorithms.

evidence.title: Using a Machine-Learning Algorithm to Identify Palliative Care Needs in a Primary Care Population: A Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported mismatch between referral alerts and patient-care timing
evidence.effect: Among 28 responding PCPs (response rate, 30%), 6 (21%) reported that alert timing did not align with patient care; 2 (7%) disagreed with the recommendation.
evidence.quote: In some instances, alert timing did not align with patient care ( n = 6 [21%]) or the PCP disagreed with the recommendation ( n = 2 [7%]).

evidence.quote: Of 66,200 GDRs generated, 21,073 were presented, and 2,264 (11%) were used.

evidence.title: Sisyphus' Alert: The Uphill Struggle to Improve Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis Clinical Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Workflow mismatch reflected in negative user feedback
evidence.effect: The wrong person receiving the alert accounted for nearly 50% of negative submitted user feedback, despite logic intended to target the patient's primary team.
evidence.quote: Review of narrative feedback and its classification highlights "wrong person" receiving the alert being by far the most prevalent cause for negative submitted user feedback (nearly 50%), despite efforts to develop logic that limits firing to the patient's primary team.

evidence.title: Evaluating the usability and practicality of AI-enabled smartphone-based obstetric ultrasound in Sierra Leone: a mixed-methods study
evidence.outcome: Workflow integration and clinician workload during deployment
evidence.effect: Providers reported easy integration and reduced workload, but observations found overload: at least 60 pregnant women per day per facility, maximum three staff, and a healthcare provider-to-client ratio of 1:23.
evidence.quote: However, despite claims of reduced workload, observations revealed that healthcare providers were often overwhelmed due to high demand for ultrasounds.

evidence.title: Investigating the Clinical Value in Relation to Implementation and Use of an AI-Generated Fracture Algorithm Tool to Support Clinical Decision-Making
evidence.outcome: Time delay between radiograph acquisition and availability of AI report in ED workflow
evidence.effect: Value stream analyses showed a 6-23 min delay between radiograph acquisition and availability of the AI report; authors note workflow integration still requires improvement.
evidence.quote: Value stream analyses showed a delay of 6-23 min between radiograph acquisition and availability of the AI report.

evidence.title: Sequencing AI Automation and Data Interoperability in Oncology Using a Scenario-Planning Framework Coupled With Discrete-Event Simulation: Proof-of-Concept Study
evidence.effect: Automation islands had worse performance: RTTI 37.1 days (+26% vs 29.4 baseline) and throughput 647/year vs 1022/year.
evidence.quote: While the trajectory toward S IV showed a combined increase in efficiency (lower RTTI) and number of treated patients, S II resulted in higher RTTI and reduced throughput, suggesting that AI automation intensity may become counterproductive when isolated from data interoperability.
evidence.sample_unit: stochastic simulation replications per scenario coordinate

commentary.bottom_line: Three studies suggest that AI components fitting existing workflows are used more and disrupt less, but none tests whether assessing fit before purchase changes uptake, burden, or patient outcomes. Fourteen hazard studies document low uptake and added burden when fit is poor, which supports the concern but does not show that the recommended assessment solves it.

perspectives.view: The one real-deployment test is a quasi-experimental study in which components built into pharmacist workflows were used and reduced antimicrobial use, while a new multistage hand hygiene behavior failed. The other two tests are offline simulations. No study compares pre-purchase fit assessment with no assessment, so certainty is very low because of design and indirectness.

Wrong-recipient alerts accounted for nearly 50% of negative user feedback in one deployment, and charge nurses documented acknowledgment of alerts in 18.6% of cases in another. Alerts that go unread may allow deterioration to pass unnoticed. No study shows that a pre-deployment fit review prevents these failures.

Utilization averaged 29% in one trial, with a separate EHR tab cited as a barrier, and 11% of presented message drafts were used in another deployment. Workload scores rose from 43 to 57 after one rollout. A reader study found concurrent AI reading cut mean time by 13.5 seconds versus independent reading, which suggests integration design affects burden.

None of the three tests reports Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. In Sierra Leone, observers found a provider-to-client ratio of 1:23 despite reported easy integration, and in Kenya duplicative paper-based data entry was the main barrier to adoption. These findings suggest fit problems may be larger in low-resource settings.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks what else users might be doing at the same time, and a multi-society radiology statement says workflow integration must be considered. These documents are endorsements rather than binding duties for deployers, and no supplied study evaluates whether following them changes outcomes.

A simulation found that isolated automation raised time to treatment to 37.1 days from 29.4 and lowered throughput to 647 from 1022 per year. Another simulation estimated a 4% drop in daily patient volume or 2% longer operating time. A Danish emergency department recorded 6 to 23 minute delays before AI reports were available.

Primary care physicians reported excessive prompts and added cognitive and emotional strain, and 21% of responding physicians in one trial said alert timing did not match patient care. Burdened clinicians may have less attention for patients, although no supplied study measured patient-reported effects.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments that underwent structured pre-purchase assessment of workflow, technology fit, user acceptance, and clinician burden with deployments that did not. A prospective multisite comparison that measures uptake, clinician workload, and patient outcomes, and that includes safety-net and limited English proficiency settings, would address this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the three studies testing the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations; only a hazard study in Sierra Leone included limited English proficiency and rural populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume the findings transfer to their staffing levels and workflows.
